Last seen on vinyl in 1990, Clock DVA’s scuzzy blast of noirish skronk, spangled psych and cold war spy funk for Throbbing Gristle’s Industrial Records remains a wicked relic of a pivotal 1980 and exemplary of Adi Newton’s expansive vision - RIYL James Chance & The Controtions, Suicide, Cabaret Voltaire.

‘White Souls In Black Suits’ was recorded by an early iteration of CDVA led by an Adi Newton who a few years earlier had departed The Future, a prototype of The Human League, and was beginning to embark one of late C.20th electronic music’s most fascinating projects. The eight-part album captures Newton (voice, synth, clarinet, bowed electric guitar, and tape treatment) blaring beside Clock DVA co-founders Steven James Turner, David J. Hammond, Charlie Collins, Roger Quail, and Simon M. Elliott-Kemp, with Cabaret Voltaire’s Steven Mallinder & Richard H. Kirk overseeing from the studio booth at their Western Works Studio. Aye, lad, it’s a proper Sheffield thing, like vinegar buns, cutlery and inclines.

At the fore Adi Newton’s vox channels a troubled soul of late ‘60s garage psych and late ‘70s goth and industrial qualities, comparable to Gen P-O as much as Takashi Mizutani and Peter Murphy, but with his own prowling, scowling swagger binding their songs, stepping from th clipped cold wave funk of ‘Consent’ and fuzzed up sleaze of ‘Discontentment (1 & 2)’, thru 10 mins of lysergic, strung-out psych mumble and caterwaul on ‘Non’. They hit a needling, wiry ace with ‘Relentless’, and sow seeds for CDVA’ oddest tangents and fascinations with “surveillance, obsession, and psychological decay” with the soundscapes of ‘(Film Soundtrack Keyboards Assemble Themselves at Dawn)’ and atonal collage ‘Anti-Chance’.

100% killer reissue of Bim Sherman’s self-released 1988 dub masterpiece ‘Ghetto Dub’, mixed by King Tubby, Prince Jammy and Adrian Sherwood who diffuse rhythms by The Roots Radics and Sly & Robbie, newly remastered for its first new edition in 30 years.

With 2nd hand prices understandably climbing into triple figures, this overdue first vinyl reissue will be mana to the fiends. It takes pride of place in an ongoing programme of resurrected Sherman aces to portray him at his most elusive and atmospheric, or as the hype sticker calls it, “a journey in echo and space”.

His legendarily tone is threaded thru the desk by a team of JA/UK titans with the man himself in the producer role, sifting cuts from his Century Records: a label set up in the Uk in 1984, after his move from Kingston, JA, to London, where he became a crucial figure in the On-U Sound crew after joining their 1979 tour, and would lend to classic Dub Syndicate cuts among others. 

The record’s renown has grown over the years since Sherman’s passing in 2000 and the effective dissolution of his label. Week-End Records now do a sterling job of preserving his legacy with this edition, richly representing the warmth and pressure of the OG in its entirety, from the clean-spurred, buoyant step of its title tune to moon-booted ‘Untitled Dub’, via the soul-tugging ace ’Station Dub’ with its unanswered doorbells, and best showcase of his voice in ‘Moving Dub’, another alright stepper in ‘World Dub’, the bloozy wooze of ‘Danger Dub’ and wickedly skewed Afro-lilt of ‘Tribulation Dub.’

All killer.

At the age of 72, "Evil" Graham Lee, the legendary pedal steel pioneer and veteran of the iconic Australian band The Triffids, delivers his first ever album under his own name titled ‘I Think I’m Alone Now’.

"In addition to his work with The Triffids, Graham’s place in ambient history was cemented in 1990 when his evocative pedal steel became the soulful centerpiece of The KLF’s masterpiece, Chill Out (specifically on the highlight “Baltimore to Fair Play”).

I Think I’m Alone Now is a profound exploration of the instrument's emotional range, blending traditional country infused melodies with vast, reverb drenched ambient textures. The album spans six tracks, anchored by the Side B title track, a 15 minute textural piece that leans heavily into the ambient genre. From the delicate melancholy of "Seeking Beauty in Sadness" to the curious abstraction of "Nursery in the Beehive," Lee uses his pedal steel and an array of pedals to sculpt unique, haunting soundscapes that exist between tradition and the avant garde.

The connection is brought full circle with exclusive liner notes written by The KLF’s Bill Drummond. Reflecting on a forty year friendship that began when The Triffids served as the backing band for Drummond’s solo debut, The Man, Drummond provides a personal and poignant context for this long awaited solo bow."

Snapshot of multigenerational free jazz jams by a trio of lauded Far East artists, bringing together Japanese pianist Masahiko Satoh, Korean saxophonist Kang Tae-Hwan and Japanese percussionist Midori Takada.

"Recorded during a memorial concert for the influential critic and producer Soejima Teruto, TON・KLAMI documents a unique meeting between three pioneering artists whose individual careers helped redefine the possibilities of improvised and experimental music across Japan and Korea from the late twentieth century onwards.

Masahiko Satoh is one of the most influential figures in post-war Japanese jazz and experimental music. Across a career spanning more than six decades, he has continually expanded the possibilities of improvisation through work encompassing jazz, contemporary composition, electronic music and interdisciplinary collaboration.Kang Tae-Hwan is a foundational figure in Korean free improvisation and one of the most distinctive saxophonists to emerge from East Asia. His radical approach to breath, tone and extended technique has influenced generations of improvisers internationally. Midori Takada is internationally celebrated for her groundbreaking work as a percussionist and composer. Her recordings and performances have profoundly shaped contemporary understandings of minimalism, rhythm and environmental sound, earning renewed global recognition in recent years.

TON・KLAMI reflects 33-33's ongoing commitment to uncovering overlooked histories within experimental music. Through a catalogue spanning contemporary commissions, archival recordings and cross-cultural

collaborations, the label seeks to create new contexts for significant work that sits beyond conventional genre boundaries. In bringing this recording back into circulation, 33-33 continues its wider exploration of artistic exchange between Japan, Korea and the international avant-garde. A rare document of spontaneous dialogue between pioneering improvisers Masahiko Satoh, Kang Tae-Hwan and Midori Takada, exploring tension, texture and space through cross-cultural experimental sound."

Japanese noise metal punk Viviankrist’s solo debut of 2019 pitches her somewhere between Merzbow and Russell Haswell with a torrent of tart, distorted oddities for Cold Spring.

Originally issued the same year as her Diagonal album, which shares a quota of unruly electronic DNA, ‘Morgenrøde’ pays witness to the singular, radical artist renewing an early alias after decades playing in black metal (Gallhammer), sludge grind (Congential Hell), and dark ambient (Sehnsucht, with Maniac & Andrew Liles) bands. Taking the reins solo, Viviankrist summons a slew of sour sounds, staking out charred power electronics on ‘Silent Soul’,  and no wave synth bin juice in ‘Spring Song’, along with Merzbow-esque beat noise in ‘Spite Spits’ and ‘Pleasure of Confusion’. But the bets bits are reserved to her more explicitly electronic ones, from the curdled arp steeple and decay of ‘Morgenrøede’, thru the Haswellian acid-electro of ‘Cactus’ and a chattering ‘Higher Minded’ that feels like CoH gone analog.

In the realm of impromptu recordings that fully transcend the moment, ‘Mary In Voice Memo’ is one of the loveliest things we’ve heard in ages. A set of one-take songs for voice and piano captured on an iPhone with no overdubs or edits, it’s an elevated document of snatched conversations and location recordings that bleed into a set of heartfelt songs for the ages. It reminds us of Dominique Lawalrée’s brittle parlour music via Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru’s transcendent, off-the-cuff ‘Souvenirs’, and Klein’s opaque songs of worship, transposed to a contemporary Nebraska. 

Lawson spent a decade recording as Mesonjixx before eventually finding unexpected freedom through these personal recordings, made between 2020 and 2025. She set herself a few simple rules; recording everything in a single take and only using reverb, delay and pitch to free herself from contemporary production churn. The goal was to channel feeling with unvarnished immediacy, and the resulting ‘Mary In Voice Memo' is a revelation, soft hued and vulnerable, but brimming with a level of emotional resonance rarely heard in improvised music. When she breaks into song on opener 'BATHE ME', Mary’s voice is dented by familiar ambiance: cars driving by, wind hitting the microphone, distant hammering that becomes a kind of rhythm. On 'M+D', her piano is captured loosely to convey the feel of the room as much as the notes themselves. Her voice only appears for a moment, to remind us she's still there.

The album winds through Lawson's life, a pseudo rehearsal with marching minimalism on 'EVEN IN THE DARKEST TIMES', splicing musical elements through a recollection of an offhand conversation with a lover. These moments bolster the album's narrative, so when we hear a more florid track, like the gorgeous 'Bridge of Red Hat Litancy of Voices', we understand that it's spilling out from the same place right at the top of the dome. The short, candid recitals like 'WE'LL BE ALRIGHT', balance out the album's more poignant tracks like 'O'BLESS ME NOW', a poem embedded in slow, reverberating chorals. And it's the album's last track, 'SURELY GOODNESS X EVEN IN X' that hands us the key to the entire record, when Lawson walks us from her home to church, singing solo before the entire congregation send her off. 

It's a moving denouement to an album that's been played here daily since we first encountered it, evoking similar feelings to when we first heard Virginia Astley’s ‘From Gardens Where We Feel Secure’, or more recently those timeless room recordings by Salenta + Topu, gently wafting into the room as we dip in and out of it’s unique reveries. In other words; a low key discovery of the year.

Whew! A who’s who of contemporary aces rework one of 2024’s strongest LPs, with everyone from Anderson Do Paraiso to Fauzia and Kelman Duran exerting canny spins on Nídia & Valentina’s sticks-meets-circuits polyrhythmic jams.

All hewing faithful to the originals, but delineated in compelling mix of club-ready styles, the remixers prove the classy contemporary mutability of ‘Estradas’ by dare-to-differ batida/tarraxho artist Nídia, and her prolific spar, Valentina Magaletti, who is resoundingly acclaimed for work with literally everyone in the modern scene. 

To play faves, DJ Anderson do Paraíso’s gothic baile spin on ‘Andiamo’ is a clear frontrunner, adding his own vox and illuminating bonds between Portuguese-speaking Afro-Latin diaspora, whilst Fauzia also kills with the glute-twang bassline of her ‘Nasty’ version, and Felt label boss Fergus Jones impresses with his dubbed-out slant on Valentina’s drumming in a ‘No Promises Version’.

Safe to say the rest do not let the side down, with Beyoncé producer Kelman Duran reframing ‘Ta A Bater Ya’ as a heady collage of after-the-storm ambient noise and spectral drums, and Rosa Pistola x Freebot proving ideal remixers for the horny sapphic twiss-up ‘Rapido’, and DJ Plead gets right entangled in the additional layers of percussion to his ’Sicilia Version’. Even Sherelle makes a noted progression from primary colour jungle to ruder, textured nuance on wicked 160BPM version of the title tune.

Landmark, evergreen debut by the eternally charming singer-songwriter, ushering bossa into the emerging tropicália sound in ’67, on a round of songs laced with a political bent that would see him and Caetano Veloso locked up by the military regime in ’69...​

"Arriving on the eve of Tropicalismo, the record places Gil’s guitar at the center of rich arrangements by Carlos Monteiro de Souza, Dori Caymmi, and Leonardo Bruno. Blending samba, bossa nova, carnival traditions, and Northeastern Brazilian rhythms, the album explores social, political, and religious themes. The title track “Louvação,” co-written with Torquato Neto, calls for collective awareness, while “A Rua” carries a bittersweet nostalgic tone. Gil’s deep connection to Bahia flows through “Beira-Mar” (with Caetano Veloso), and his poetic imagination shines in “Lunik 9,” reflecting on the space race. “Ensaio Geral” captures the political energy of carnival, while “Rancho da Rosa Encarnada” (with Torquato Neto and Geraldo Vandré) evokes traditional festivities. Highlights include the rhythmically inventive “Roda,” the celebratory “Viramundo” (with Capinan), and the nostalgic “Água de Meninos.” The romantic “Maria (Me Perdoe, Maria)” offers a moment of intimacy, while “Procissão” closes the album with a powerful reflection on faith and society."

A longtime regular on Future Times and Mood Hut, and also known as half of Aquarian Foundation, Tanner Matt really flexes a ruffer range on Newroomfreak’s eponymous debut. Aside to a pair of gunky beat-less and beatdown works, its all about the full bore rave pressure here, authentically emulating a heyday of ’92-’93 breakbeat hardcore with the brutal body animator ‘Newroomfreak [WIDE]’ calling to mind the Amiga-squashed breaks of early Chaos & Julia Set via Jega’s Skam gems, whereas ’40z’ gets looser, splashier with the breaks in widescreen mode, where his ‘New Out’ wriggles for 10 mins of tail-chasing breaks and flyaway flute licks to get teeth and feet gnashing at the bit.

items.body:
Maiden vinyl reissue for a cult 1971 slab of cool and vibrant spiritual jazz by flautist Hadley Caliman and pianist Todd Cochran aka Bayeté, who would go on to play keys/synths for Herbie Hancock, Peter Gabriel, Aretha Franklin.

“Wewantsounds continues its reissue program of Bob Shad's cult jazz label, Mainstream Records, with Hadley Caliman's superb 1972 album, Iapetus. Recorded in LA and featuring a heavyweight lineup of West Coast players including Todd Cochran, Woody “Sonship” Theus, Luis Gasca, and Victor Pantoja, the majority of the album was composed by Todd Cochran (aka Bayeté) soon after he had composed Bobby Hutcherson's Blue Note classic, Head On. A true hidden treasure, it is reissued here on vinyl for the first time since 1971, featuring its original gatefold artwork with rare first-generation photos. This edition comes with newly remastered audio and a two-page insert with exclusive liner notes by Todd Cochran, reflecting on Hadley Caliman and the making of the album.”

items.body:
A wealth of DIY dubplates and 45s from Jah Massagan’s East London sound crop up for first time on tape with cherry-picking label Death Is Not The End - heavy roots dub troubles cut at the studios of King Tubby, Lee Perry, Channel One, and Joe Gibbs…

Eljay Mass, son of Jah Massagan’s owner-operator, Lloyd Mass, dips into his dad’s enviable archive for an hour of rare, one-away platters that hail a self-organising rhizome of sound systems which sprang up in the UK with arrival of the Windrush generation, and brilliantly altered the course of music on this strange island in the process. 

The cassette-only session speaks to prevailing links between Caribbean culture and UK inner cities which reverberated from the ‘70s into the ‘80s, and has endured as a touchstone for some of our isles’ most vital music, setting templates for independent distribution networks and producing waves of innovative hybridisation.

Owner-operator Lloyd Mass and his childhood pal and amp builder Tony Mass were a small but steadfast part of preserving these sounds, holding down their Leyton corner of London, where they would pass the torch to Eljay Mass and an extant network of rigs, engineers, Deejays and ravers who really do it for the culture.

items.body:
Ernestas Kausylas does scuzzy motorik krautrock, stoner Can-type jams, garage sleaze and widescreen space rock on his 2nd LP with ace Amsterdam label South of North.

‘Lima Echo Crack!’ finds Brokenchord drift farther from electronic moorings into classic, late C.20th guitar, drum and vocal song forms drenched in FX scuzz, as found on his pivotal ‘Stone Island Tracks’. More confident in his combustible drive here, the eight tracks are also not without a hash-head pathos that tempers his mission. 

In ever increasing circles, it turns open out from the motorik propulsion of ‘Prowler’ to 11 mins of full strung-out, lysergic space rock on ‘Liquid Mind Experiment’, dialling it down to a more opiated groove on ‘MKUltra Scarecrow’ and the slackened Neu! 2 B-side styles in ‘CRACK!’ and ‘Get Lost’, before arriving at an expansive mountain-top panorama in ‘PBR’, revving up for the final straits in the dubbed out, grinding ace ‘Tomorrow knows’.

French club music sculptor (Marine) Benabou comes into her own on a handful of rolling pressure systems backed with Kliche’s dub-diffused breakbeat remix.

Slotting very neatly into Blank Mind’s roster of sparing dance engineers - Lina Filipovich, Paperclip Minimiser, DJ ojo - the Berlin-based producer brings her background as mastering/cutting engineer at ManMade to the fore on a rangy EP. The precision-tooled, syncopated percussion and stereo-strafe grayscale movement of opener ‘Projet G’ establishes parameters where she moves freely into vaporised dub techno (‘Interlude’), to something approaching Sandwell District gone samba in ‘Rise’, and restless forms of sinuous, sidewinding suss in ’Shift’, while ‘Merge’ demonstrates her feel for lucid, resonant clarity and depth perception. Label mate Kliche flexes ‘Projet G’ in a dubbier antechamber style in step with DJ ojo aces.

items.body:
Hot on the heels of their ‘Junglist!’ set, Soul Jazz reload their anthem-studded 2007 comp, packing early-mid ‘90s hardcore and ragga jungle heat by M-Beat & General Levy, Ragga Twins, SUAD, Cutty Ranks x DJ SS.

‘Rumble In The Jungle’ tells the story of jungle’s rapid evolution from mutant hip hop x dancehall in the late ’80s, via hardcore, to its hugely distinctive ragga and jump-up phase of the mid ‘90s. It’s a baga sounds that successive waves of producers have attempted to emulate ever since, but simply doesn’t get better than the OG tackle, as Soul Jazz well know.

The Ragga Twins understandably dominate the set with three bullets, the foundational, acid dancehall rap of ‘Ragga Trip’, sped-up fast rap steez of ‘Illegal Gunshot’, both from 1990, plus the ragga techno of ‘Tan So Back’ (1992), which all sparks so many dances and imaginations BITD. Shut Up and Dance, who issued all the above, are also on board, but with the gummy 2000 garage of ‘No Doubt’, which is hardly a standard, but does show how the sound had muted 10 years later.

The rest is all dead solid as a primer for inquisitive junglists/junglettes, firing General Levy’s alternative national anthem ‘Incredible’ and the murderous DJ SS remix of Cutty Ranks’ ‘Limb By Limb’, beside lesser known but wicked zingers such as DJ massive’s clattering hardcore rufige in ‘Final Conflict’, a deep fried steppa by The Source, and of course X Project’s deadly ramp of Beenie Man & Barrington Levy’s ‘Under Mi Sensi’.

items.body:
Finally following up 2019's cult tribal reconstrucción 'System', Delia Beatriz trades hauntology for rhythmic momentum on 'Potpourri', imagining a parallel timeline where guarachero evolved in conversation with acid house and dub techno, fusing its fundamental tresillo reticulations with caustic 303s, Chain Reaction-style echoes and ferocious psychedelic distortions. RIYL Dengue Dengue Dengue, Verraco, DJ Babatr, Safety Trance, British Murder Boys or Lechuga Zafiro

Beatriz has always balanced her dedication to the dancefloor with higher minded obsessions; even her debut album, 2018's NAAFI-released 'Animus', was a 50/50 split of rhythmic experiments and intoxicating soundscapes. But since combing the distant past on 2022's 'The Long Count' and her own musical autobiography on last year's cumbia rebajada love-letter 'Desaceleradas', the forward-thinking club hybrids that reached their peak on 'System' have taken a back seat. Thankfully, she picks up the trail on 'Potpourri', auditing her technique while simultaneously critiquing the past, present and future of Latin dance music. The conceptual rigor that anchored her last run of releases is intact, but 'Potpourri' is an album for the dancers, first and foremost, an arsenal of rave weapons that conspicuously straddles a conflicted border. Even the cover, surreptitiously shot on the bridge between the USA and Mexico, reflects the album's provenance, its grafting of genetic material sourced from Detroit, Chicago, Mexico City and Monterray.

'System' was an attempt to blend tribal guarachero with industrial techno and 'Potpourri' focuses the concept further, burying its roots deeper in techno's subsoil. Over an album length this time, Delia considers the fast-paced, non-linear way tribal legend Javier Estrada worked to redevelop her approach to writing club music from the ground up. "It's a manifesto for rethinking form and sound in dance music," she explains. "By stepping outside traditional structures and embracing the potpourri approach, I'm creating new meaning with familiar rhythms." We can hear exactly what that means on the cheekily-titled 'Assimilate', when familiar syncopated thuds plunge through a heaving mass of 303s, forming a compound that's part Jeff Mills, part Chico Sonido. But it's that high end that has us properly gripped; Beatriz knows that it ain't just kicks that'll infuse her potpourri so peppers in aromatic tresillo shakers, cutting almost to silence at the track's halfway point to make sure we fully comprehend the pyramid.

Similarly, on '2placesatonce', her corrupted hoover sounds and square wave bleeps are neatly offset with bass tangs and woody acoustic percussion, everything cooked in a layer of grizzled distortion. It helps, no doubt, that the album was mixed by Berlin-based club alchemist Ziúr, who waves her magic wand over the material and gives it the punch it needs to really dominate, whether it's on headphones or belting out of a full Function One setup. And that's completely necessary; just as 'Desaceleradas' was concerned with the feeling of nostalgia evoked from certain phrases or tonalities lifted from cumbia rebejada, 'Potpourri' is driven by the energy that runs through classic club records from both sides of the border. It's music that needs to be experienced on a physical level, inspired by potent memories and powered by Beatriz's desire to keep the contemporary scene evolving or, at the very least, searching.

On their third album, Henry Birdsey's New England collective submerge windswept Americana in dense, oddly-tuned dronescapes, meditating on folk's origins and future eventualities by stirring banjo and slide guitar phrases with abyssal reeded wails and grungy tape loops.

Best known for his subterranean work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor, Birdsey is one of the New England scene's most prolific operatives. 'Dissection Maps' comes only moments after last year's mossy 'Sewn the Name', and picks up where its predecessor left off. There's a different cast this time around (though how many of the contributors are Birdsey's pseudonyms we can't tell you), but the result is largely similar. Birdsey (or J.M. Eagle) plays banjo, pedal steel, bagpipes and resonator guitar, and takes the lead throughout, jangling over Ann Rowlis' organ, bells and rattles on opener 'Sleeps With Dice', the album's straightest nod to its roots. Things start to disintegrate on 'Singing Loom' when the discernible riffs are traded for magickal sustained tones that seem to melt into one another. It's not clear exactly what instrument is playing or when, but Addison Starkweather-Price's harmonica is a constant, and we're sure we can hear bagpipes in there somewhere.

Reana Doram steps in to add ghostly hammered dulcimer chimes to the gusty 'Dealt in Silver', playing against Grainger Farnsworth's doom-y electric bass punctuations and Rowlis's chilling organ and bells, and she shows up again on the mind-bending closer 'Last Rings', adding galloping rhythms to Ryder Tarbox's fluttering tape loops.

The sublime spirit of Satie endures in Yumiko Morioka’s 1987 landmark of Japanese ambient and modern classical, originally ushered at a time when she was moonlighting in pop songwriting for male idol singers, and has been known to trade for triple figures, even on its 2020 repress. Simply beautiful music FFO John Adams, Brian Eno, Erik Satie.

"Recorded on a Bösendorfer grand piano, much of Resonance was made in an attempt to soothe her creative soul. Constructed from unwritten improvisations with additional instrumentation added later, Resonance explores the space between notes. As such, it's a record that feels open and inviting, permeated throughout with a sense of confident serenity.

The sparse, delicately played notes are allowed to reverberate and echo through the spaces between themselves, giving each track a feeling of both grandeur and intimacy. Like the great pioneers of classical and ambient music, there's a timelessness to Resonance - a comforting, familiar feeling, as if these melodies have always existed.

Resonance drew influence from the popular environmental music culture prevalent in Japan during the late 80s, but it was also heavily inspired by Western musicians such as the avant-garde Parisian composer Erik Satie. Listening today, it still feels fresh and pertinent; a warm, contemplative reflection of a travelled woman."

items.body:
Downbeat and deep house mavericks, Steve Cobby & Dave McSherry, cough up a deluxe, remastered expansion of their ’94 debut LP as the 2nd classic offering from Forever Records’ reliquary.

Last on wax in 2002, ‘Old Codes New Chaos’ now returns to circulation as an expanded edition. It all ideally portrays the Humberside duo at an early crest of their powers, dovetailing the UK’s prevailing threads of ambient and deep house, chill-out music, and more whimsical indie, with a signature wit and relative outsider charm that can possibly be attributed to their roots in Hull, where they would be cited as a formative cue for likes of Richie Culver (although you may need to squint your ears to get that). More generally, and with the benefit of hindsight, they can be heard as very symptomatic of ‘90s halcyon days, when a new wave of youth found their dancing feet, and needed a soundtrack to cushion rave comedowns of this type. 

Following on from Forever Records’ PWOG reissue (crafted on the opposite side of the North Sea a few years earlier), ‘Old Codes New Chaos’ shares a similar thing for grooving sensuality and atmospheric levity, but with a pastoral English touch that can’t help but evoke bucolic summers and likely induce huge nostalgia from those there at the time, or likewise in the eternal now. Front to back it’s balmy pleasure to stroll from the siren calling deep house swag of ‘Mermaids’ thru the harmonic glow of ‘New Chaos’, taking in the Weatherall-style swagger of ‘Brazilification’, or K&D type lounge music of ‘The Sheriff’, to the 18 min electro-dub-house collage of ‘Fila Funk.’

items.body:
Oh man, quite possibly the oddest, cutest thing we’ve heard this year - cult Japanese underground duo Tenniscoats sing and play over a bunch of iconic hip-hop and r'n'b instrumentals on an hour-long tape for A Colourful Storm’s choice Fleetway Tapes sublabel; a concept that’s so brilliantly wtf that we were sold before they even droped a beat.

Saya and Takashi Ueno have never confined themselves to a single genre over the years, bending softer-than-soft whimsical folk, indie pop and psych rock into their own unique shapes - but we still could never have imagined them produce anything like this. We can't tell you how Moopie managed to convince them to yank it from the archives, but it's a total joy - the most eccentric record in Tenniscoats' already distinctive catalogue. 

There's a level of warm fuzz that emphasises the mix was beamed in from another decade - the tape crackles to life with melodica wails that hang remarkably well over the sturdy, bass-heavy instrumental from Mobb Deep's 'Quiet Storm', the lead single from the foundational duo's misunderstood fourth album 'Murda Muzik'. It isn't an obvious track ('Temperature's Rising' or 'Shook Ones, Pt. II' would have been the casual's choice), but it's a stone-cold killer, boasting some of Havoc's dirtiest bass and a snare that could cut glass. Saya does her best to ad-lib her own rap at first, eventually settling into a sort of soft-hued spoken word that floats Havoc's beat from the Queensbridge projects all the way to Tokyo. 

Their take on TLC's 'No Scrubs' is even weirder, with Saya's fragile vocal turn and Takashi's fittingly flamenco-inspired acoustic guitar pushing the overfamiliar beat gently into new territory. You could say 'Hip Hop Tennis' is a karaoke mixtape of sorts, the kind of selection of hastily-made reworks and versions that used to litter the streets outside Brooklyn's Broadway Junction or down on the Lower East Side before the coffeeshops and Cronut stores moved in. But Saya and Takashi's impromptu jams elevate this into the sublime, as if they'd put together a mix of East Coast favourites in the early '00s and spontaneously added their own ingredients on top. Just check the duo's dubbed-out rhymes over Brand Nubian's 'Word Is Bond' or Saya's loungey turn on the underrated Neptunes-produced banger 'Light Your Ass on Fire' and you’ll know exactly what we’re saying.

It's a session that's brimming with a palpable affection for its influences; the first side ends with a lengthy half-speed Nuyorican love-in, and then the second bursts open with an uncharacteristically nursery rhyme-like flip of The Inc's low-key Ashanti-starrer 'No One Does It Better'. Saya's blustery, saturated wails even transform Eve's enduringly popular Dre-produced 'Let Me Blow Ya Mind', while Takeshi attempts to sand down the edges of DMX's 'X Gon' Give It To Ya'. But the best moment comes when Takeshi plays in a minor key over Jeru the Damaja's 'Come Clean' - probably the best East Coast hip-hop track of the '90s - completely re-contextualising it, and trust when we say we thought we'd heard every which way that track could be flipped. 

Even if you've been following Tenniscoats since 2000's 'The Theme of Tenniscoats' - you ain't ever heard them like this.

Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.

Returning after a decade-long break with none other than Isis/Sumac frontman Aaron Turner at the helm, Neurosis move into a new era with their sickest album since the iconic 'Through Silver in Blood'. Tipped!

It would have been easy to assume that Neurosis would have folded after guitarist and vocalist Scott Kelly, one of the band's founder members, was dismissed following domestic abuse allegations. Indeed, as late as in January last year, it looked like things were fizzling out when drummer Jason Roeder claimed he was ready to sell his music equipment and retire from touring. And it would have made sense, too; Neurosis have been active since the mid-1980s and defined a sound that would evolve into "post-metal", pulling influence from hardcore, prog, industrial music, ambient and sludge and inspiring a legion of followers. They never really lost their mojo, either - even their last album, 2016's Steve Albini-recorded 'Fires Within Fires' was pretty universally regarded as one of that year's best metal releases. But truth be told, they'd started to repeat themselves; locked into Kelly's grim, agonized lyrics, they were starting to sound like their own gloomy tribute act. If it was the end, they'd had a good run.

So 'An Undying Love...' is in many senses a total surprise Not only is the band back, re-energised, but they have a new vocalist and guitarist in tow: Turner, whose old band Isis were arguably the most important members of post-metal's second wave. You might consider the new Neurosis lineup as the ultimate post-metal supergroup, then, and 'An Undying Love...' is the record that proves the credentials of everyone involved. Unlike its tight, almost too brief predecessor, this album is a return to the epic, sprawling songwriting that both Neurosis and Isis perfected at their respective peaks. And it's incredibly expansive, too; anyone who's been following Turner in recent years will already know how open-minded he is, whether it's with his work with Moor Mother and Keiji Haino as Sumac or his various genre-bending collaborations. Here, there's an extra layer to the Neurosis sound that fills out their sludgy, lurching epics with the meticulously engineered haze of Isis's milestone 'Oceanic'.

Where Neurosis's last few albums had been shaped by their long-time collaboration with Albini, this one sounds like a clean break, mixed and recorded by Oakland's Scott Evans, who worked on Turner's Sumac records. It's still Neurosis, with those slow, almost symphonic atmospheres and the unmistakably tight rhythm section, but there's even more going on here, whether it's the unsettlingly effective breakdowns that often replace the band's usual instruments with synths and pounding drum machines, or the stacked feedback loops and scratches that fill their riffs with even more tension. Turner's lyrics, too, offer the band a new dimension to explore. "The separation that burns our hearts / is the root of all our disease," he bellows on the opener 'We Are Torn Wide Open' over radio interference. "We've forgotten how to live so we suffer." Self-referential in their own way at first, they move on as the band does, rolling through themes of environmental collapse, division and redemption. 

It's worth it just for the payoff delivered by the album's side-long finale 'Last Light', shifting from hi-BPM dark gabber into pure symphonic sludge, using its hefty runtime to properly display what this nu-Neurosis (NeurIsis?) is capable of. Really, it's not just the band's most vital record in years, it's one of the best metal albums we've heard in way, way too long.
